basics.title: Text and mathematics in one answer
basics.text: Write explanations as ordinary paragraphs. Put a short mathematical expression between one dollar sign on each side, as in $x+1$. For an expression on its own line, put two dollar signs on each side. The dollar signs are editing markers and disappear in the preview. The Insert math button supplies a pair and places the cursor inside. You can keep using handwriting instead; neither answer is erased when you switch.

basics.title: Commands, spaces, and literal characters
basics.text: A TeX command begins with a backslash followed by its name. Command names are case-sensitive. A space ends a command name: without it, following letters become part of the name. Ordinary spaces inside mathematics are usually ignored. Spaces in normal prose are kept. To print a dollar sign, type a backslash immediately before it instead of opening math. Syntax help explains each supported command; this editor handles mathematical expressions, not entire LaTeX documents.

basics.title: Braces group input
basics.text: Braces tell a command or notation marker which characters belong together. Grouping braces do not appear in the rendered result. Each opening brace needs a closing brace. If you want a brace itself to appear, use a backslash followed by that brace. Commands that need input show their required groups in Syntax help.

basics.title: Type a superscript
basics.text: A caret raises the following input into a superscript. Often this is an exponent; in other notation the lesson explains a different meaning. Without braces the caret applies only to the next character. Use braces around a multi-character superscript: x^{12} raises x to twelve, while x^12 raises it to one and then writes a separate two. This grouping rule matters even when the preview looks superficially plausible.

basics.title: Type a subscript
basics.text: An underscore introduces a subscript, printed below the baseline. Use braces when its label has more than one character. An exponent and a subscript can both follow the same symbol. Their mathematical meanings are supplied by the lesson; these editing markers only control their position.

basics.title: Rows and columns
basics.text: For a table of mathematical entries, start a matrix environment and close it with the same name. Within it, an ampersand separates columns and two backslashes finish a row. Every row should have the same number of entries. Use pmatrix for surrounding parentheses or bmatrix for square brackets. An aligned environment uses the same separators to line up successive equations; cases supplies a left brace for case-by-case expressions. An array also takes a column specification such as {cc}. These are typesetting arrangements, not new mathematical operations.

basics.title: Reading the editor feedback
basics.text: Commands are blue, braces brown, operators green, and subscript/exponent markers purple. Matching braces highlight near the caret. An underline signals syntax needing attention, such as a missing closing brace. This is not a mathematical correctness check. It is normal for an expression to be temporarily incomplete while you type. Your exact draft is saved even when the preview cannot render it. Use Undo to reverse an edit; the preview never edits your source.

basics.title: Type exactly-one existence
basics.text: Type the exists command followed immediately by an ordinary exclamation mark: \exists!x. There is no separate exists-with-exclamation command. Here the exclamation mark belongs to the uniqueness notation explained above; it does not request a factorial. Parentheses still determine which predicate the notation applies to.

basics.title: Type paired vertical bars
basics.text: Use the vertical-bar key on both sides of the expression, as in |A|. No backslash is needed. Here the bars mean cardinality, as defined above; elsewhere they may mean absolute value. The typed characters do not by themselves decide the mathematical meaning.

basics.title: Visible set braces and a condition
basics.text: Every brace that you want printed needs its own backslash. This also applies to nested sets. In a set-builder description, type the colon as an ordinary keyboard character between the element expression and its condition. Grouping braces without backslashes still serve only the editor.

basics.title: Type a set complement
basics.text: Use the superscript marker and the letter c: A^c. The c is a single-character superscript so braces are optional; A^{c} is equivalent input. This is the complement notation explained above, not raising a set to a numerical power.

basics.title: Type an infix relation
basics.text: When the relation is named R, type its name directly between its two inputs: aRb. R is an ordinary letter here, not a backslash command. Use ordinary parentheses and a comma for the corresponding ordered pair. The relation definition above determines which pairs belong.

basics.title: Type an equivalence class
basics.text: Use ordinary square-bracket keys around the representative: [a]. Do not add backslashes before these brackets. If a relation label is needed, append a subscript, as in [a]_R. The brackets denote the class defined above; they are not a list of its members.

basics.title: Keep minus one together
basics.text: Type the inverse marker as ^{-1}, with both the minus sign and 1 inside the braces. Writing ^-1 would raise only the minus sign and leave the 1 on the main line. Here the superscript labels the inverse operation explained above, rather than a reciprocal.

basics.title: Type a function specification
basics.text: Type the function name and an ordinary colon, then its domain, the to command, and its codomain: f:A\to B. To state the output rule for an individual input, use mapsto instead: x\mapsto x+1. These two arrows play the different roles explained above.

basics.title: Type an interval
basics.text: Use ordinary parentheses or square brackets for interval endpoints. A square bracket includes a finite endpoint; a parenthesis excludes it. An infinite endpoint uses the infty command and a parenthesis. Mixed endings such as [2,\infty) are intentional and do not indicate a missing bracket.

basics.title: Type a preimage
basics.text: Type f^{-1}(T), keeping minus one together in its superscript group. With a target set T this is the preimage notation explained above, even when an inverse function does not exist. The same visible superscript can therefore have a context-dependent meaning.

basics.title: Type a restriction
basics.text: To label the restriction of f to an input subset S, type f|_S: an ordinary vertical bar followed by the subscript marker and S. This means the same rule evaluated only on S, as explained above. For a longer label use braces after the underscore.

basics.title: Keep the whole index together
basics.text: Write a_{n+1} with the entire index inside braces. The plus one belongs below the baseline. Writing a_n+1 would instead add one to the term. The subscript labels which term to use; it is not multiplication.

basics.title: Limits and the summand
basics.text: After the sum command, put the starting index equation in an underscore group and the ending index in a caret group. Then type the summand. Group a multi-character upper limit such as n-1. Parentheses around the summand make its scope clear; braces after the sum command do not automatically print parentheses.

basics.title: Type a factorial
basics.text: Type an ordinary exclamation mark immediately after the input: n!. There is no factorial command. For a compound input, use parentheses: (n-1)!. Unlike the earlier exists-with-exclamation notation, this exclamation mark denotes the factorial operation explained above.

basics.title: Separate the limits of nested sums
basics.text: Write each sum command with its own lower and upper groups, followed by the term being added. The second sum can use the first index in its limits. With a two-index term, put both indices and their comma inside one subscript group. Follow the outside-to-inside evaluation described above.

basics.title: Line up a calculation
basics.text: Use the aligned environment for a calculation with several lines. Put an ampersand immediately before the equality sign on each line and two backslashes between lines. Close the environment with its matching end command. The layout helps a reader follow a proof, but it does not supply a reason for any step: write those reasons in the surrounding paragraphs. In this example, assume a=2r and b=2s for integers r and s; the first line substitutes those assumptions, and the second factors out 2.

basics.title: Type vertices and edges
basics.text: Type V and E as ordinary capital letters. To list undirected edges, each edge is a visible pair of braces inside the visible braces of the whole edge set; every printed brace needs its own backslash. For a directed arc use an ordered pair with ordinary parentheses instead. A typed list of edges records the connections even without a sketch.

basics.title: Type the letter O
basics.text: Big O uses the ordinary capital letter O, not the digit zero and not a backslash command. Put the comparison expression in parentheses, as in O(n^2). This displays the eventual-bound notation explained above; the parentheses do not mean multiplication by O.

basics.title: Type the lowercase letter o
basics.text: Little o uses an ordinary lowercase o, not zero. Write o(n) with the comparison expression in parentheses. The distinction between lowercase o and uppercase O matters mathematically. Use varepsilon for the epsilon in the definition; its name begins with a backslash and is followed by a space before ordinary letters.
